what_happened.line: The Select Board voted 5-0 to extend the health insurance opt-out pilot program through fiscal year 25.
The board deferred its vote on the Building Commissioner's new fee schedules for building, electrical, plumbing and gas permits, to allow two weeks of public review.
The proposed schedules raise the commercial rate and minimums, move sheet metal permits to a per-thousand rate, and raise the plumbing and gas fees set in 1987.
The board ratified, 5-0 by roll call, a police sergeant promotion and the appointment of an assistant town accountant.
The board heard two public comments with complaints about the police chief and the cemetery commission chair.

why_it_matters: Anyone pulling a building, electrical, plumbing or gas permit, or applying for a stop work or occupancy permit, could pay different fees if the schedule is adopted, and the vote has not yet happened.
The opt-out pilot extension keeps in place the arrangement that the board tied to the public employee committee agreement, which bears on what the town spends on employee health insurance.

The Building Commissioner's report back, about a year later, on how the new fees are working.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted to recommend most draft special town meeting articles, including a roof repair, two sewer stabilization transfers and the Marshall Park article.
Six articles (A, B, C, D, N and P) were deferred to next week, ahead of the warrant signing deadline.
The board recommended the primary school cooling systems article (E) on a 3-1 vote, with one member objecting to the choice of system.
At a joint meeting, the Select Board and Parks Commission appointed a new Parks Commissioner through May 2024 by roll call.
Public commenters sharply criticized the tax investigation team, and the board began a bylaw review, voting to replace 'selectman' with 'select board' in chapter 74.

why_it_matters: The articles recommended here, covering school cooling, a roof repair, sewer reserves and ARPA funds, are the ones residents will be asked to vote on at special town meeting, and the Select Board's recommendation will appear beside them.
Six articles still have no recommendation, so what they would ask of taxpayers is undecided until the board returns to them next week.
watch_next: The deferred articles A, B, C, D, N and P are to be revisited next week before the warrant signing deadline.
Board members are to review the remote participation policy (chapter 305) and chapter 5 bylaws for the October 24 meeting.

The board added the farm bylaw and articles on common driveways, solar canopies and water supply protection, and referred the planning articles to the Planning Board for hearing.
The animal bylaw was pulled from the special town meeting and deferred to spring; the board then voted unanimously to include all other draft articles.

The board signed a one-year bond anticipation note, and a public speaker challenged the board over an open meeting law finding against the tax investigation team.

why_it_matters: The articles now on the warrant are the ones residents will be asked to vote on at the Special Town Meeting, including a co-response clinician that could draw on opioid settlement money rather than the tax levy.
The bond anticipation note is short-term borrowing that comes back for renewal, and the open meeting law finding bears on how the town's tax investigation work is conducted in public.

Next week's agenda, which is to carry the open meeting law determination response or appeal; the minutes note a 21-day appeal period.

The dangerous-dog order sets restitution and insurance conditions on the owner and gives the board a basis to hold a new hearing if the conditions are broken.

The board heard ARPA requests from the Library, the food pantry and the Boys and Girls Club, then agreed generally to allocate some ARPA funds to most pending requests.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted to suspend On the Rocks' liquor license for 10 days, May 19 through May 28, with five business days to appeal to the ABCC.

Before the suspension, the board found violations on alcohol sales law, standards of conduct (selling to under 21) and Mass General Law chapter 138 section 34; a finding on the environs of the premises failed 2-2.
The board agreed to commit ARPA funds for Marshall Park construction and for consulting and reporting, and said it would revisit further requests later.
A request about a handicap parking spot and paving at 243 Summer Street was deferred with no decision; members will research and follow up.
The board approved a peddler's license for a solar solicitor and heard the town manager on ARPA vehicle purchases, vacancies and bids.

why_it_matters: ARPA money is a one-time pot, so each commitment to a park, a consultant or a department request uses funds that cannot be spent twice and that no tax bill replaces.
The board still holds requests from the schools, the water district, sewer, police and the food pantry, so the order in which they are funded decides which of those projects go ahead.
watch_next: The town manager's consolidated list of ARPA commitments and open items, and further information requested from the school, sewer, police and food pantry groups.
The town manager evaluation composite expected the following week, with the vote the week after that.

The chair floated holding the hearing after the pending violation hearing; the board instead decided the transfer that night.
The board ratified a new Building Commissioner and a part-time police administrative assistant.

A floor amendment at Town Meeting will strike 'residential' from Article 21 section three, so reallocation applies to all taxpayers.

why_it_matters: The license transfer went ahead while a violation hearing on the same establishment was still pending, so that hearing's outcome now bears on a license already held by the new owner.
The fire union contract carries annual raises and other pay changes with stated yearly fiscal impacts, and Town Meeting voters will be asked to approve it as Article 8.
The Article 21 amendment, as described in the minutes, changes whether a reallocation applies to residential taxpayers only or to all taxpayers, which touches how a tax bill is divided.
watch_next: Town Meeting votes on Article 8 (the fire union contract) and the Article 21 amendment.
The solar license applicant is scheduled for 7:10 at next Tuesday's Select Board meeting.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted to recommend two annual town meeting articles: prior year invoices paid from free cash, and the FY2024 sewer enterprise budget.
The sewer enterprise budget was revised to cut capital spending to cover Fitchburg rate increases and retiree costs, and the board recommended it.
The auditors presented the FY22 audit, with federal awards audited with no findings and the town's pension and retiree health liabilities both described as lower.
The board spent a long stretch on Flat Hill Road drainage with no resolution; the engineer will look at a modified detention system in the town right of way and size the land needed.
The board appointed a 300th anniversary committee member and ratified the town manager's seasonal beach staff appointments.

why_it_matters: The two recommended articles, one drawing on free cash and one setting the sewer budget, go to residents at annual town meeting, where they will be asked to vote on them.
Any fix for Flat Hill Road flooding that needs land or a detention system would be a capital cost to the town, and the minutes give no cost or funding source for it yet.
watch_next: Engineer's sizing of a modified detention system and the land it would need on Flat Hill Road.
Annual town meeting votes on articles 3 and 14, and on the opioid stabilization article, which Town Counsel is reviewing.

what_happened.line: The Select Board deferred a Marshall Park funding request that included federal pandemic relief (ARPA) money, targeting May 9 to take it up.
The Parks Commission presented its Marshall Park cost to date, phased construction estimates and funding scenarios; the board voiced support but made no commitment.
The board voted to amend an earth removal permit by removing land sold for a warehouse, leaving the remainder under the permit.
The board accepted the fire chief's changes to the emergency management plan and appointed a member to the agricultural commission.
The board agreed to a consent calendar of town meeting articles with article one removed, then went into executive session on fire union bargaining.

why_it_matters: The Marshall Park project could be paid for with ARPA money, with borrowing, or with grants, and which mix is chosen affects how much debt lands on the tax levy and the town's debt policy limit.
A late invoice for last year's stormwater coalition membership would be paid from free cash, which raises the free cash used in the budget that town meeting will be asked to vote.
watch_next: May 9: the date the board targeted to take up the Marshall Park ARPA funding request.
April 25: the next Select Board meeting; none is scheduled for next week.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted 4-0 to recommend most Town Meeting warrant articles, including the omnibus budget, capital plan, stabilization, OPEB and senior tax relief.
The board deferred the firefighters union contract article and the sewer enterprise budget, the latter because the Sewer Commission has not voted its final number.
In a joint workshop, the Board of Assessors voted 3-0 to set January 6 as the mailing date for the third and fourth quarter tax bills.
The board asked the assessors for a written abatement review process within about a week, with a published schedule.
Residents pressed on abatement hearings, a land value increase and the timing of decisions, and the board also made three appointments.

why_it_matters: The January 6 mailing date sets when the later tax bills are due and when interest begins, and the unsettled abatement process decides how and when residents can contest their assessments.
The recommendations and deferrals shape what voters will be asked to approve at Town Meeting, including the budget, reserve transfers and the pending firefighters contract and sewer budget.
watch_next: The assessors' written abatement review process and published schedule, due within about a week.
The deferred articles on the firefighters union contract and the sewer enterprise budget, and the Town Meeting votes on the warrant.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to treat FY23 tax bills as mailed in January, making May 1 the due date, once Town Counsel hears from the state Department of Revenue.
The board approved committing ARPA funds to public safety building security cameras and to help the Board of Assessors with assessment services.
The board accepted the updated Nashoba Valley Regional Dispatch District agreement, 3-0 with one recusal.
The board approved the Howard Street pole relocation after a resident objected to the plan, and accepted Town Counsel's response to an open meeting law complaint.
The board reviewed FY24 capital and warrant articles, deferring recommendations to next week, then entered executive session.

why_it_matters: The mailing-date vote decides whether the abatement filing window has closed, which affects residents contesting their assessments, especially lakefront owners who raised concerns at the meeting.
ARPA money is being used for assessment services and building security, and the FY24 capital plan and warrant articles drawing on stabilization and free cash will go to a town meeting vote.
watch_next: Town Counsel's confirmation that the Department of Revenue allows the January mailing date, on which the vote depends.
Next week's meeting, where the town manager presents budget and capital numbers and the board makes recommendations, and the Board of Assessors is again invited.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted to authorize a spend on outside tax assessment services from committed funds, a stopgap while a new bid process is prepared.
The board heard long, critical public comment on the FY23 land assessment increase, including calls for the assessor's method and a public workshop.
The board and Finance Committee met the state delegation on earmarks, Chapter 70 and Chapter 90 aid, special education reimbursement, 40B and senior tax relief.
The board ratified two town manager appointments unanimously and tabled a third, a director, pending personnel committee review.
Town counsel is to draft a senior property tax relief home rule article for discussion and a placeholder on the warrant next week.

why_it_matters: The FY23 land assessment dispute bears on individual tax bills and abatement filings, and the stopgap contract suggests the investigation is not yet resolved.

Whether the state raises aid and special education reimbursement, and whether a senior tax relief article reaches the annual town meeting warrant, affects how much falls on local property taxes and who gets relief.

After the first motion was not audible, the board continued the package store license transfer hearing to February 21 at 7:15 PM once the applicant agreed.
Most of the meeting was a status update and public questions on the FY2023 property assessment investigation, including the town manager's role and abatements.

The APDC override placeholder is an article residents may be asked to vote on at annual town meeting.

what_happened.line: The Select Board moved to open an investigation under section 3-2e of the Town Charter into the FY23 assessments and the valuation and billing process; the vote was not captioned.
Officials told residents they need not pay more than a formula-based amount by Feb 1 to preserve abatement rights, with worksheets to be posted on the town website.
The town manager is to issue requests for proposals for outside assessors and arrange staffing for the assessor's office, with support in place by late February or March 1.
The principal assessor explained the mass-appraisal method, and residents questioned the assessors and board at length.
Public comment, moved to the end of the agenda, included requests for a senior cap and a resolution of no confidence in the assessment outcome.

why_it_matters: Lakefront owners facing sharply higher FY23 assessments have a Feb 1 payment point tied to abatement rights, and abatements granted beyond the overlay reduce town revenue and can touch the town budget, mostly taxes.

The charter investigation and outside assessors may change how the valuation and billing process is run, and the open question of whether abatement applicants can add information after Feb 1 affects every applicant.
watch_next: The board's roadmap and timeline for the charter investigation, and routine updates to residents.
The town website answer on whether abatement applicants may add information after Feb 1, and the outside-assessor requests for proposals.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to open the annual town meeting warrant on January 10, 2023, to close March 20, 2023 at 4 pm.
The board accepted a donated sign at McNally Field to the parks commissioners, unanimously.
The board took a position supporting state policy that lets boards choose remote or hybrid meetings without being required to provide them; the vote result was not audible.
The town manager outlined FY24 target budget assumptions, including rising health insurance, liability and retirement costs and a new police contract.
Residents told the board their tax bills had risen sharply and urged others to check bills and appeal; one asked about a senior tax credit.

why_it_matters: The warrant is the list of articles residents will be asked to vote on at town meeting, and its open window is when a petition or request can be added.

The FY24 assumptions name the cost pressures (health insurance, retirement, contracts) that the next tax bill will reflect, and residents raised assessment increases and a senior tax relief idea now headed for a possible May article.
watch_next: Warrant closes March 20, 2023 at 4 pm.
Senior means-tested tax relief goes first to the tax relief group, aimed at a May warrant article; legislative fiscal priorities due by end of January.
